changes.before: We initially examined three fungal G protein-coupled receptor involved in ascaroside sensing: Gpr2 and Gpr3 [2], and GprC [3]. We prepared receptor and ligand inputs using published pocket locations, contact residues and docking procedures as references. The AlphaFold 3 receptor structures used in docking and molecular dynamics were predicted locally with the official model parameters and reference databases [1]. We also considered their use in yeast. GprC has been reported at both the plasma membrane and mitochondria in its native fungal host [3]. We considered this a potential complication for localization and pathway integration in yeast, so we focused subsequent engineering on Gpr2, continued to investigate Gpr3 and its variants, and retained GprC as a structural reference. Initial checks revealed two input problems. Inconsistent coordinate frames between receptor structures and docking boxes displaced the search region from the intended pocket. Loss of chemical information, including formal charges, during format conversion also affected the identification of charged contacts. These findings made input validation a routine part of the workflow. We used structural superposition to place receptors, ligands, and docking boxes in a common coordinate frame, then checked the search region against membrane orientation and the receptor segments retained for docking. Atom mapping was used to check atom identities and coordinate correspondence between the original ligand SDF files and the PDBQT files. When the required Meeko metadata were retained in the PDBQT output, we exported the docked poses to SDF while restoring the original bond orders and formal charges for contact analysis [4]. Subsequent mutant comparisons used consistent ligand inputs and search settings. Original residue numbering was preserved so that docking scores could be traced to residue contacts. Published studies guided receptor selection and structural comparisons; input checks established consistent computational conditions; and docking with both ligands guided the design and screening of variants.
changes.after:
We initially examined three fungal G protein-coupled receptor involved in ascaroside sensing: Gpr2 and Gpr3 <sup>[2]</sup>, and GprC <sup>[3]</sup>. We prepared receptor and ligand inputs using published pocket locations, contact residues and docking procedures as references. The AlphaFold 3 receptor structures used in docking and molecular dynamics were predicted locally with the official model parameters and reference databases <sup>[1]</sup>. We also considered their use in yeast. GprC has been reported at both the plasma membrane and mitochondria in its native fungal host <sup>[3]</sup>. We considered this a potential complication for localization and pathway integration in yeast, so we focused subsequent engineering on Gpr2, continued to investigate Gpr3 and its variants, and retained GprC as a structural reference.

Initial checks revealed two input problems. Inconsistent coordinate frames between receptor structures and docking boxes displaced the search region from the intended pocket. Loss of chemical information, including formal charges, during format conversion also affected the identification of charged contacts. These findings made input validation a routine part of the workflow.

We used structural superposition to place receptors, ligands, and docking boxes in a common coordinate frame, then checked the search region against membrane orientation and the receptor segments retained for docking. Atom mapping was used to check atom identities and coordinate correspondence between the original ligand SDF files and the PDBQT files. When the required Meeko metadata were retained in the PDBQT output, we exported the docked poses to SDF while restoring the original bond orders and formal charges for contact analysis <sup>[4]</sup>.

Subsequent mutant comparisons used consistent ligand inputs and search settings. Original residue numbering was preserved so that docking scores could be traced to residue contacts. Published studies guided receptor selection and structural comparisons; input checks established consistent computational conditions; and docking with both ligands guided the design and screening of variants.

changes.before: This section documents the biological materials and experimental methods used in wet-lab work. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid are the nucleic acids represented in the sequence entries. We summarize the designed single-guide ribonucleic acid sequences, constructed plasmids and engineered strains generated in our project. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) underpins the cloning workflows described below. The chassis species is Saccharomyces cerevisiae; Escherichia coli (E. coli) is used for plasmid propagation.

changes.before: We developed the NemaKlear interactive web tool to explore this question. It connects ordinary differential equation (ODE) simulations of color development, dual-channel density estimation, and economic analysis. Users can select simulated soil samples or enter paired absorbance readings, estimate target nematode density, and compare net income across management strategies for a single growing season.
